1.title: Neptune, the Planet Found by Math
1.text:
Neptune, the Planet Found by Math

Neptune was discovered in 1846 after astronomers used the law of gravitation to predict where an unseen planet must be.

Our big question for this lesson: how does gravity affect objects that aren't touching? Let's start with a planet that was found with a pencil before it was found with a telescope.

William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781 with a telescope he built himself. By 1830, it was clear that the law of gravitation wasn't correctly predicting Uranus's orbit. Two astronomers proposed that Uranus was being pulled by the Sun and also by an undiscovered planet. In 1845 and 1846 they calculated where that planet should be, and in 1846 astronomers at the Berlin Observatory found it. We call it Neptune. So how do planets like Neptune and Uranus stay in orbit around the Sun?

2.title: Newton's Cannon
2.text:
Newton's Cannon

An object is in orbit when it falls toward Earth at the same rate that Earth's surface curves away beneath it.

Sir Isaac Newton used a drawing like Figure 10 for a thought experiment. Picture a cannon perched high on a mountain, firing a cannonball horizontally. The cannonball is a projectile, with horizontal and vertical motion, so like every projectile under Earth's gravity, it follows a parabola and falls back to the ground.

Fire it faster, and it lands farther away, but it still lands. Now imagine a truly powerful cannon. The cannonball would travel all the way around Earth and keep going, because it falls toward Earth at the same rate that Earth's surface curves away. Its path keeps matching Earth's curve, so it never gets closer to or farther from the ground. The cannonball is in orbit!

Newton's thought experiment ignored air resistance. To truly escape it, the mountain would need to be more than 150 kilometers tall, far taller than Mount Everest's 8.85 kilometers. At 150 kilometers, you're above most of the atmosphere, so a cannonball, or any satellite, at or above that height can orbit Earth with little or no air resistance.

4.title: A Satellite's Speed and Period
4.text:
A Satellite's Speed and Period

A satellite's orbital speed is v equals the square root of G m sub E over r; its period is T equals 2 pi times the square root of the cube of r over G m sub E.

A satellite that stays the same height above Earth moves in uniform circular motion. Its centripetal acceleration is a sub c equals the square of v divided by r. So Newton's second law, F sub net equals m a sub c, becomes F sub net equals m times the square of v, divided by r.

Gravity supplies that net force. If Earth's mass is m sub E, set capital G m sub E m over the square of r equal to m times the square of v over r. Solve for the speed, and you get: v equals the square root of capital G m sub E divided by r.

A satellite's orbit around Earth works just like a planet's orbit around the Sun. The planet's period was T equals 2 pi times the square root of the cube of r over capital G m sub s. So for a satellite around Earth, T equals 2 pi times the square root of the cube of r over capital G m sub E.

These equations work for any object orbiting another. Just replace m sub E with the mass of the central body, and let r be the distance between the two centers. And here's a neat fact: orbital speed and period don't depend on the satellite's mass at all.

testIt.name: Orbit dial
testIt.how: Drag the orbit radius and read the speed and period. Tap the satellite to change its mass: nothing changes.

5.title: Example Problem 2, Orbital Speed and Period
5.text:
Example Problem 2, Orbital Speed and Period

Find the orbital radius first: r equals h plus r sub E.

A satellite orbits Earth 225 kilometers above the surface. Earth's mass is 5.97 times 10 to the 24th kilograms and its radius is 6.38 times 10 to the sixth meters. What are the satellite's orbital speed and period?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the situation, showing the height of the orbit. Known: h equals 2.25 times 10 to the fifth meters, r sub E equals 6.38 times 10 to the sixth meters, m sub E equals 5.97 times 10 to the 24th kilograms, and capital G equals 6.67 times 10 to the negative 11 newton meters squared per kilogram squared. Unknown: v and T.

Step two: solve. First find the orbital radius by adding the height to Earth's radius: r equals 2.25 times 10 to the fifth meters plus 6.38 times 10 to the sixth meters, which is 6.60 times 10 to the sixth meters. For the speed, v equals the square root of capital G m sub E over r. Substitute capital G, m sub E equals 5.97 times 10 to the 24th kilograms, and r equals 6.60 times 10 to the sixth meters, and v comes out to 7.77 times 10 to the third meters per second. For the period, T equals 2 pi times the square root of the cube of r over capital G m sub E. Substitute the same values, and T is 5.34 times 10 to the third seconds. That's about 89 minutes, or 1.5 hours.

Step three: evaluate. Are the units correct? Speed comes out in meters per second, and period in seconds. Yes!

testIt.name: Height to speed
testIt.how: Set the height above Earth. The walkthrough adds Earth's radius, then finds v and T.

6.title: Earth Science Connection, Landsat
6.text:
Earth Science Connection, Landsat

A more massive satellite needs more force to launch, so a rocket's power limits a satellite's mass.

The Landsat 8 satellite in Figure 11 is part of the Landsat series of satellites that have imaged Earth's continents since 1972. Landsat images help people make maps, study land use, and monitor resources and global changes. They even let researchers watch small-scale processes, like deforestation, across the whole globe. Landsat 8 circles Earth about 14 and a half times a day, once every 99 minutes.

Large rockets accelerate satellites like Landsat 8 to orbital speed. Every mass obeys Newton's second law, F sub net equals m a, so a more massive satellite needs more force to launch. That means a satellite's mass is limited by the rocket that carries it.

7.title: Real-World Physics, Geosynchronous Orbit
7.text:
Real-World Physics, Geosynchronous Orbit

A geosynchronous satellite orbits once a day, so it seems to hover over one spot on Earth.

The GOES weather satellites orbit Earth once a day at an altitude of 35,785 kilometers. Their orbit keeps pace with Earth's rotation, so to someone on the ground, the satellite seems to hover above one spot.

That's handy! A dish antenna on Earth can point at one place in the sky and stay put while the satellite orbits.

testIt.name: Geosynchronous

8.title: Free-Fall Acceleration Away from Earth
8.text:
Free-Fall Acceleration Away from Earth

Free-fall acceleration at distance r from Earth's center is a equals g times the square of r sub E over r.

Newton's law of universal gravitation and his second law together tell us the acceleration of a falling object. For an object of mass m, the force is capital G m sub E m over the square of r, and that equals m a. So a equals capital G m sub E over the square of r.

On Earth's surface, a is g and r is r sub E, so g equals capital G m sub E over the square of r sub E, and m sub E equals g times the square of r sub E over capital G. Substitute that for m sub E back in the free-fall equation, and capital G cancels. You get: a equals g times the square of r sub E over r.

On the surface, r equals r sub E, so a equals g. But as you move farther from Earth's center, r grows and the free-fall acceleration shrinks with the inverse square relationship. And what happens to your mass as you go farther out? Nothing! Your mass stays the same. Only the gravitational force on it gets smaller.

testIt.name: Lift it higher
testIt.how: Drag the height. The free-fall acceleration drops as 1 over r squared.

9.title: Weight and Weightlessness
9.text:
Weight and Weightlessness

Apparent weightlessness happens when you and everything around you fall freely together, so no contact forces push on you.

You've probably seen photos like Figure 12, with astronauts floating in a so-called zero-g environment. Their spacecraft orbits about 400 kilometers above Earth. At that height, g is 8.7 newtons per kilogram, only a little less than on Earth's surface. So Earth's gravity is definitely not zero there. In fact, gravity is what keeps the craft in orbit! So why do the astronauts seem weightless?

Remember, you sense your weight when something, like the floor or a chair, pushes on you with a contact force. If you, your chair, and the floor are all accelerating toward Earth together, nothing pushes on you, so your apparent weight is zero. The astronauts and their craft are all falling freely toward Earth. The floor is constantly falling away from beneath their feet!

Gravity is still very real up there. A 75.0-kilogram astronaut 405 kilometers above Earth, where g is 8.7 newtons per kilogram, feels a gravitational force of 75.0 kilograms times 8.7 newtons per kilogram, or about 650 newtons.

testIt.name: Box ride
testIt.how: Tap the box to ride from the ground to orbit and into free fall. Watch the scale reading.

10.title: The Gravitational Field
10.text:
The Gravitational Field

A gravitational field surrounds every object with mass; its strength is g equals G m over the square of r.

Many forces you know are contact forces, like friction or the push of a chair. Gravity is different. It acts on a falling apple and on the orbiting Moon. It acts over a distance, between objects that aren't touching. Newton himself was puzzled by this. How could the Sun pull on Earth from hundreds of millions of kilometers away?

The idea that explains it is the field. Michael Faraday developed the field concept in the nineteenth century while studying magnets. Gravitational, electric, and magnetic fields explain forces that act at a distance.

Every object with mass is surrounded by a gravitational field. Another object feels a force from the interaction between its own mass and the field g at its location. The field points toward the center of the object making it, and its strength is g equals capital G m over the square of r, where m is the mass of the object making the field and r is the distance from its center.

testIt.name: Field probe
testIt.how: Move the probe's distance and direction. The field vector always points to the planet's center.

11.title: Measuring and Picturing the Field
11.text:
Measuring and Picturing the Field

The gravitational field is the force per unit mass, g equals F sub g over m, measured in newtons per kilogram.

Suppose the field comes from the Sun. A planet of mass m feels a force F sub g equals m g, toward the Sun. The force comes from the planet's mass interacting with the field right where the planet is, not with the Sun millions of kilometers away. If more than one object makes a field, find each field and add them as vectors.

To measure a gravitational field, place a small test mass m in it and measure the force on it. Then g equals F sub g over m, in newtons per kilogram. On Earth's surface, g is 9.8 newtons per kilogram, pointing toward Earth's center.

Figure 13 pictures Earth's field as a collection of vectors all pointing toward Earth, getting shorter as you move away, following the inverse square relationship. The field depends on Earth's mass, not on the mass of the object feeling it. Why does g never reach zero? Because one over the square of r gets smaller and smaller as r grows, but it never actually becomes zero, no matter how far you go.

testIt.name: Test mass on a scale
testIt.how: Change the test mass and the distance. F changes, but F over m stays the field strength.

12.title: Two Kinds of Mass
12.text:
Two Kinds of Mass

Inertial mass measures resistance to acceleration; gravitational mass measures response to gravitational force.

You learned that mass is the slope of a force versus acceleration graph: net force divided by acceleration. This kind of mass is tied to inertia, so it's called inertial mass. In symbols, m sub inertial equals F sub net over a.

It's much easier to push an empty cardboard box across the floor than one full of books. The full box has more inertial mass. Inertial mass measures how much an object resists a change in its motion. You measure it by applying a force and measuring the acceleration. The more inertial mass, the less acceleration a given net force produces.

Newton's law of universal gravitation also involves mass, but a different kind. Gravitational mass measures how strongly an object responds to gravitational force. You can measure it with a simple balance, like the one in Figure 14. If you measure the attractive force F sub g on an object from another object of mass m at a distance r, then m sub g equals the square of r times F sub g, divided by capital G m.

testIt.name: Two kinds of mass
testIt.how: Tap to push the boxes with the same force, then tap again to weigh them.

13.title: The Principle of Equivalence
13.text:
The Principle of Equivalence

The principle of equivalence states that inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude.

How different are these two masses? Say there's a watermelon in your car's trunk. Speed up, and the watermelon rolls backward relative to the trunk. That's its inertial mass at work, resisting acceleration. Now drive up a steep hill at constant speed. The watermelon rolls backward again! This time, it's because of its gravitational mass. Earth is pulling it down.

Newton claimed that inertial mass and gravitational mass are equal in magnitude. This idea is called the principle of equivalence, and every investigation so far supports it. That's why we usually just say "mass." Albert Einstein was fascinated by the principle of equivalence too, and he made it a central idea in his theory of gravity.

14.title: Einstein's Curved Space
14.text:
Einstein's Curved Space

Einstein proposed that mass curves space, and objects accelerate because they follow that curved space.

Newton's law lets us calculate gravitational forces, but Newton was puzzled about how two objects millions of kilometers apart could pull on each other. Albert Einstein proposed a different picture: gravity isn't a force, but an effect of space itself. Mass changes the space around it, curving it, and other objects accelerate because they follow that curved space.

One way to picture this is the top part of Figure 15. Model three-dimensional space as a big stretchy sheet. A large ball on the sheet, standing in for a massive object, makes a dip. Roll a small ball across the sheet, and when it passes near the dip, it speeds up and curves. In a similar way, Earth and the Sun attract each other because of how they distort space.

testIt.name: Rubber sheet
testIt.how: Set the ball's mass and tap to roll a marble past it. A bigger mass makes a deeper dip and a sharper bend.

15.title: Planes Flying North and Converging Apples
15.text:
Planes Flying North and Converging Apples

In flat space parallel lines stay parallel; in curved space they converge.

Here's another analogy. Picture watching from space as two planes fly due north from the equator, 4000 kilometers apart. As they near the North Pole, the gap shrinks to 1 kilometer. Each pilot thinks they're flying in a straight line, but seen from far above, their paths curve, because Earth's surface is curved. That's shown in Figure 15.

Now drop two apples toward Earth on parallel paths. As they fall, both are pulled toward Earth's center, so their paths converge. You can think of this convergence as the curvature of space near Earth. Far from any massive object, like a planet or a star, space is flat and parallel lines stay parallel. In curved space, they converge.

Einstein's explanation is called the general theory of relativity. It makes many predictions about how massive objects affect one another, and in every test so far, it has given the correct results.

testIt.name: Planes flying north
testIt.how: Fly both planes north from the equator. On a sphere their straight paths move together.

16.title: Bending Light and Black Holes
16.text:
Bending Light and Black Holes

Massive objects bend light; a black hole is so massive and dense that no light escapes it.

Einstein's theory predicts that massive objects bend light. Light follows the curvature of space around a massive object, as Figure 16 shows, which shifts where its source appears to be. In 1919, during a solar eclipse, astronomers found that starlight passing near the Sun was bent by the amount Einstein predicted. That's surprising, because in everyday life light seems to travel in perfectly straight lines!

General relativity has an even more dramatic result. If an object is massive and dense enough, light leaving it is bent all the way back. No light ever escapes. These objects are called black holes. We've identified them by their effects on nearby stars, and by the radiation produced when matter is pulled into them.

So how does gravity affect objects that aren't touching? Every mass fills the space around it with a gravitational field, or, in Einstein's picture, curves the space around it, and other objects respond to that field wherever they are.

testIt.name: Light near the Sun
testIt.how: Slide the Sun's mass. Starlight grazing it bends by an angle that grows with the mass.

17.title: Scientific Breakthroughs, Making Waves
17.text:
Scientific Breakthroughs, Making Waves

Gravitational waves are ripples in space-time that travel at the speed of light.

In 1916, Einstein used general relativity to predict gravitational waves, ripples in space-time traveling at the speed of light. Nobody detected them on Earth until 2015, when two Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatories, or LIGOs, one in Louisiana and one in Washington, picked them up for the first time. The waves came from two black holes that collided and merged into one bigger black hole about 1.3 billion years ago. As they merged, some of their mass was converted into energy, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E equals m times the square of c, and that energy was carried away as gravitational waves.

In 2017, the two American LIGOs and a similar detector in Italy, Advanced Virgo, detected another black hole collision, from about 1.8 billion years ago. With three observatories, scientists could triangulate the waves and pin down where the collision happened more precisely. That same year, the three observatories detected gravitational waves from two colliding neutron stars, about 130 million years ago. This time, scientists studied both the gravitational waves and light across the whole electromagnetic spectrum. The stars kept glowing for weeks after their collision!

In 2017, three physicists won the Nobel Prize for their key contributions to detecting gravitational waves. This research opens a new window on violent cosmic events, like colliding black holes. Your challenge: with a partner, research how a LIGO works, then draw or build a model that shows how it detects gravitational waves, and present it to your class.

testIt.name: Interferometer
testIt.how: Tap to send a gravitational wave through. One arm stretches, the other squeezes, and the fringes shift.
